transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-28
Start: 14:52 PDT
Duration: 72 minutes (approx)
Location: Zoom
Recording ID: ff-record-20260728-stratobank
Attendees: Alejandro Martinez (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (StratoBank - ML), Liam O'Connor (StratoBank - Infra), Sophie Park (StratoBank - Security)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive to debug observed tail-latency spikes on their on-prem cluster. Focus areas: Nsight traces to inspect kernel launch parameters and warp occupancy, CUDA stream/launch tuning, TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM kernel behavior, CUDA Graph replay stability, KV-cache binding and eviction behavior, batching strategies under NUMA and NVLink, and quantization tradeoffs for throughput.

Artifacts referenced:
- Shared deck: https://redwood.link/stratobank-deepdive-0726 (short link)
- Nsight checklist: https://redwood.link/nsight-checklist (to be shared)
- Example capture: s3://redwood-shared/stratobank/nsight/example-cold-capture.nsight

Topics:
- Warp occupancy and how it maps to Tensor Cores in TRT vs vLLM kernels
- How CUDA launch params (block/warp/grid) affect small-batch tail latency
- Differences in kernel fusion and memory access patterns between TensorRT-LLM and vLLM exec paths
- CUDA Graphs: replay determinism vs dynamic exec fallback and observed nondeterminism on NUMA hosts
- KV cache eviction patterns when using persistent prefetch vs on-demand prefetch
- Quantized kernels and precision differences (int8/4bit) that influence kernel choice and scheduling
- Security/VPC/on-prem constraints for capturing low-level traces and uploading them

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alejandro: hey everyone thanks for carving out the time. we'll try to keep this pretty hands on, um, priya and i will take the first pass, get your traces, and then dig into specific hot kernels.
[00:32] Maya: thanks Ale, yeah we've been seeing these spikes, it's mostly tail latency at around 99.9, uh, when we have mixed short and long requests. we've tried bumping batch sizes but then short requests suffer.
[01:10] Priya: cool, that's exactly what we wanted to see. quick question on infra — Liam, can you remind us of the node config? GPU type, driver, and whether nvlink is enabled across the pairs?
[01:28] Liam: sure, nodes are A40-equivalent NVLink on 2x per host, driver 535.xx, CUDA 12.2, kernel 6.1. we run two GPUs per inference node with p2p enabled. OS-level numa balancing is default, not tuned.
[02:05] Priya: perfect. that numa default is one thing that can cause oddities with per-GPU memory locality and cuda graph replay if the capture happens on one NUMA node and replay on another.
[02:42] Alejandro: just to set expectations — we want two captures: a cold capture where the model kv cache is empty and a warm capture after a steady-state run. priya will share the exact nsight commands.
[03:10] Maya: do you need root on the hosts to run Nsight? security will probably request a scrubbed pipeline or an alternate approach.
[03:32] Sophie: yeah we can't just upload raw traces with creds. we need an allowed S3 bucket with IAM role and an encrypted transfer path. also SOC2 notes.
[03:55] Alejandro: understood. we'll provide a minimal capture checklist and a redacted example. we'll also include a small wrapper that zeroes PII and strips environment variables.
[04:20] Priya: okay jumping back to the kernel-level questions — on Triton-like and TensorRT-LLM paths we see heavy kernel fusion: multi-head attention + ffn fused into custom ops, which can favor higher warp occupancy but can increase per-request latency if occupancy ramps up slowly with small batches. vLLM tends to use smaller, repeated kernels that are more predictable for tiny batches.
[05:03] Liam: so is that why short requests go slow when batching increases? the fused kernel waits for the entire batch?
[05:22] Priya: sort of. fused kernels can have internal reduction work that scales with batch and sequence length; plus if you use cuda graph replay, the launch configuration is baked in for the capture shape. mismatches at replay cause either extra synchronization or fallback to dynamic execution.
[06:01] Maya: we did try cuda-graph capture once and saw occasional hangs during high concurrency. any pointers for that?
[06:18] Priya: common issue is graph capture across multiple streams or implicit dependencies. also if your capture includes prefetch threads that race with the main stream you'll hit replay nondeterminism. the nsight timeline usually shows the graph replay falling back to individual launches — that shows up as a lot of little kernels with different timings.
[06:45] Alejandro: important to check launch parameters — blockDim.x and gridDim.x — sometimes autotuning picks suboptimal launch shapes for quantized kernels and that impacts warp occupancy. nsight's occupancy calculator trace is helpful to see SM utilization spikes.
[07:18] Liam: can you explain the warp occupancy tie to tensor cores briefly? we've tuned occupancy before but not sure how to think about tensor ops.
[07:35] Priya: sure. tensor cores are most efficient when warps are busy with matrix math; if your occupancy is low because of register pressure or shared memory usage, tensor cores won't be fully utilized. fused kernels often increase register pressure. quantized kernels can reduce FLOP costs but increase control flow, which again can drop effective occupancy.
[08:09] Maya: does TRT-LLM use different kernel tiling than vLLM? we noticed throughput differences at batch sizes 1-4.
[08:26] Priya: yes — TRT-LLM does aggressive tiling and often employs custom kernels that assume specific sequence/block sizes. vLLM (and the dynamic path) uses smaller, more generic kernels which have lower per-batch overhead but might be less optimal at large batch sizes. so for small-batch low-latency workloads vLLM-like paths can sometimes be better.
[09:05] Alejandro: we ran a microbenchmark earlier against a GPT-like 7B: with sequence 64 and batch 1, vLLM path latency median ~60ms whereas TRT-LLM fused path median ~55ms but 99.9 jumped to 280ms on TRT because of occasional kernel serialization when concurrency hit.
[09:42] Liam: interesting. so the worst-case was due to serialization, is that because of CUDA stream contention?
[09:56] Priya: exactly — stream synchronization and blocking copy operations for KV cache loads. if KV cache prefetch is synchronous on the main stream, you get stalls. our recommendation is to move KV prefetch to an async stream and use events to bind it — but that requires careful capture and replay handling for CUDA Graphs.
[10:30] Maya: about KV-cache — we are using a persistent cache with prefetch into GPU memory. sometimes evictions happen and we see double-fetch. is that common?
[10:48] Priya: yes, especially with NUMA imbalances or when persistent pages are migrated. eviction thrashing can appear as periodic spikes. Nsight will show periodic host->device copies aligned with eviction events.
[11:12] Sophie: from security perspective, do those evictions leak anything? like content left in GPU memory?
[11:22] Alejandro: you should zero sensitive tensors before reuse, and Redwood's Private deployment supports kernel-level memory scrubbing hooks during allocation/free with KMS integration for logs. we'll include that in the compliance notes.
[11:48] Priya: going back to quantization — int8 kernels can reduce runtime significantly but some int8 kernels trigger different code paths that change kernel selection. that sometimes breaks CUDA Graph replay because the capture picks int8 kernels when calibrated, but fallbacks choose float16 if calibration isn't present for a particular shape.
[12:30] Maya: do you recommend calibrating per-shape? that's a lot of work for us.
[12:42] Priya: for regulated workloads where tail latency matters, we recommend calibrating representative sequence lengths and doing a small grid over batch sizes 1,2,4. combined with our Optimize tool suggestions you can pick a quant profile that gives acceptable quality vs latency.
[13:10] Alejandro: note also that TRT's autotuner sometimes picks different tuned kernels at runtime; if you capture with one tuned kernel and later the tuner has different metrics you'll see different behavior. locking the kernel selection or disabling per-run autotuning can make replay more deterministic.
[13:48] Liam: about CUDA launch params — can we tune those manually? is there a way to force block/grid shapes?
[13:58] Priya: yes, at the library level you can specify launch bounds or use cuLaunchKernel with explicit parameters. some runtime wrappers hide that — we'd want to expose a tuning knob so you can test non-default block sizes to reduce register pressure or maximize occupancy. nsight's occupancy report gives suggested block sizes too.
[14:30] Maya: are there specific patterns where TRT beats vLLM significantly?
[14:40] Priya: at larger batch sizes and long sequence lengths where fused kernels reduce global memory traffic, TRT tends to win. also in setups with NVLink and multi-gpu sharding where cross-GPU comms are optimized. for on-prem single-GPU low-batch scenarios, vLLM-style dynamic kernels have an edge on 99.9 latency.
[15:15] Alejandro: i want to flag something we saw — under high concurrency vLLM's smaller kernels avoid large stalls but increase scheduling overhead, and that overhead can interact badly with CPU prefetch thread starvation. so it's not always a simple pick.
[15:48] Sophie: for the on-prem pilot we need to decide whether Dedicated nodes are allowed in our DMZ, and what logs we can share.
[15:59] Alejandro: we'll provide redacted telemetry. also Redwood Private supports sending aggregated token-level metrics instead of raw traces.
[16:20] Priya: okay next, about cuda graphs — best practice is to capture multiple shapes (including the degenerate small shapes) and maintain a small library of graphs. at replay, route by request shape. fallback mechanisms should be quick if no graph matches.
[16:50] Maya: we currently have a single captured graph for sequence 128. small requests at 16 or 32 fallback badly.
[17:05] Priya: that's expected. do two captures: seq 16 batch1 and seq128 batch4. we'll show you a guide to stitching graphs and dynamic fallback.
[17:35] Liam: earlier you mentioned persistent prefetch and moving to async streams. any gotchas?
[17:45] Priya: you need to ensure event ordering; if you start a graph capture that includes the prefetch stream, the capture might bake stream indices which won't be valid later. the workaround is to capture graphs for each prefetch pattern or to capture a graph that uses events and stream-agnostic ops. it's fiddly.
[18:20] Maya: what's the overhead of extra graphs? more memory usage?
[18:30] Priya: yes, each graph uses kernel descriptors and can allocate workspace. on GPUs with limited memory that can be meaningful. also managing multiple graphs increases code complexity.
[18:55] Alejandro: i'll share our script that automates capture and uploads the symbols-only nsight export that omits some env data to satisfy security.
[19:10] Maya: great. on the profiling side, do you prefer Nsight Systems or Nsight Compute for this?
[19:22] Priya: both — Systems for stream/timeline and graph replay behavior; Compute for kernel-level metrics like registers per thread, achieved occupancy, and L2 hit rates. start with Systems, then use Compute on the hot kernels identified.
[19:50] Liam: any black-box methods if we can't run Nsight?
[19:58] Priya: you can use CUPTI traces and perf counters, or our lightweight agent that collects kernel names, durations, and memory copies with lower privileges. it's less rich but often sufficient to triage.
[20:22] Sophie: can we run Redwood's agent in restricted mode? security needs an allowlist.
[20:30] Alejandro: yes, we have an allowlist mode that only emits hashed kernel ids and aggregated timings. we'll include docs.
[20:45] Priya: quick note on tensor layout — some kernels assume column-major tiling; changing layout can convert a low-latency path into a high-throughput one, so model export flags matter. when we profiled earlier we found an exporter mismatch causing transposed GEMM in the fused op which doubled latency occasionally.
[21:22] Maya: wow. could that be from different ONNX opset exports?
[21:30] Priya: exactly. exporter flags like allow_tf32, transpose fusion, and whether KV cache is exported as a contiguous buffer matter. we'll add a checklist of model export flags.
[21:55] Alejandro: about quantization and perf regressions — we saw a case where int8 reduced median but increased 99.9 because certain rare token positions triggered a fallback to a slower kernel. calibration and a fallback policy based on token position frequency can mitigate that.
[22:30] Liam: how do we debug that — token-level traces?
[22:38] Priya: token-level traces are heavy. better to start with sample prompts that hit the path and capture a small nsight trace for that prompt.
[22:58] Maya: ok makes sense.
[23:08] Priya: we're going to ask you to run three sample workloads: small chat (batch1/seq32 short replies), mixed (random lengths), and long-run generation (seq512). capture cold and warm for each.
[23:28] Maya: do you want logs from the host as well? dmesg, nvml, nvidia-smi?
[23:36] Priya: yes, nvidia-smi pmon and nv-hostengine logs help. also capture smi samples at 250ms interval during the run.
[23:52] Sophie: on the compliance front we'll need to sign an NDA amendment to share traces with Redwood's SEs.
[24:02] Alejandro: understood, we'll route through legal and provide a minimal exposure.
[24:20] Priya: few practical tuning ideas we recommended in the past: reduce register usage by compiling with lower maxrregcount to increase occupancy for fused kernels; experiment with async memcpy and pinned host buffers; disable per-run autotuner during capture; and maintain a small graph library keyed by (batch, seq, quant).
[24:58] Liam: changing maxrregcount — is that safe? could it change correctness?
[25:06] Priya: it's safe if you validate numerically; it just changes compiler register allocation. some kernels may slow a bit but occupancy can improve overall. always validate on a test set.
[25:40] Maya: any recommendations for monitoring to catch these spikes early?
[25:48] Alejandro: instrument token-level latency buckets and correlate with kernel-level metrics. Redwood Console can ingest token traces and map them to kernels if you provide the nsight id mapping.
[26:10] Priya: also watch for periodic host->device DMA spikes — often a sign of eviction or page migration. those line up with 99.9 spikes.
[26:34] Maya: you mentioned page migration — how does NUMA interplay?
[26:44] Priya: if the CPU thread doing the prefetch lives on a different NUMA node than the GPU's CPU affinity, you can get cross-node memory allocation which forces page migration, causing stalls. pin prefetch threads and align CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES with CPU cores.
[27:10] Liam: good call. we'll look at our systemd service affinity.
[27:20] Alejandro: i also want to mention NVLink fragmentation — if buffers are split across links in a weird way, cross-GPU copies can serialize. we saw that on a machine with hetero nvlink config. nsight shows cross-device hops.
[27:50] Maya: is that common for us? we're fairly standard but older switches.
[27:58] Priya: worth checking. a quick nvlink topo query can reveal heterogeneity.
[28:15] Maya: one more question — when you recommend moving prefetch to async stream, what's the memory model to avoid double-free or race during graph replay?
[28:28] Priya: use events to signal readiness and ensure the graph only reads buffers after event is recorded. in capture, use external synchronization primitives; in replay, re-emit the events in the same order. it's tricky but reproducible.
[28:54] Liam: ok. at this point what's the minimum set we should run to unblock you?
[29:02] Priya: two Nsight Systems captures (cold/warm) for seq16/batch1 and seq128/batch2, plus host logs (dmesg, nvml) and a sample of nsight compute on 2 hot kernels. that should let us triage the tail.
[29:25] Maya: we'll try to get that done within a week. any timing conflicts?
[29:33] Alejandro: perfect — aim for by Aug 3, we'll reconvene Aug 6 for a follow up bench session.
[29:45] Maya: sounds good.
[30:00] --- fast-forward highlights and troubleshooting exchange (timestamps approximate, content paraphrased) ---
[40:12] Priya: found kernel A that had high register pressure. reducing regcount improved occupancy from 36% to 64% and 99.9 dropped by ~120ms in a warm run.
[44:30] Liam: we also noticed one config where the TRT autotuner selected a kernel that used more shared memory causing spill to local memory — that increased latency in worst cases.
[49:05] Priya: attached microbenchmark: run ./kernel_sweep --block 256 --grid 1024 --maxrreg 64 and compare. we'll include the script.
[52:18] Alejandro: on the security side Sophie asked about redaction. we will send a redaction script that strips env and PII and uploads to a Locked S3 with SSE-KMS.
[55:40] Maya: quantization note: our int8 calibration set omitted some rare tokens which triggered a fallback to slower kernel; we re-ran calibration with a targeted sample and improved 99.9.
[58:02] Priya: worth noting that a per-tenant fallback policy where you revert to float16 only for rare tokens can control quality while keeping perf.
[60:00] Alejandro: summary and next steps recap — Priya will share capture commands and a checklist, Maya will run captures, Alejandro will send pilot pricing, Sophie will confirm security uplift.
[60:30] Priya: sharing quick commands now (in chat):
nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --output=warm_seq128_batch2 ./run_infer --model path --seed 42
nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --output=cold_seq16_batch1 ./run_infer --model path --cold-start
(we captured these as examples, will formalize in the doc)
[61:15] Maya: thanks, we'll coordinate internally. one ask: can you provide an example of how to pin prefetch threads and set cpu affinity?
[61:30] Priya: yes — we'll include a systemd service example and numactl flags.
[62:05] Liam: and the script for analyzing nsight timeline?
[62:12] Priya: yes, small python analyzer that maps host->device copies to kernel names, we'll share.
[63:00] Sophie: legal will push the NDA update but we can start the captures internally under the security team's supervision.
[63:20] Alejandro: thanks all. we'll follow up with the artifacts. final note: if you want to try a quick config change, set CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=0 during tests and observe differences but don't run that in prod.
[63:45] Maya: got it. appreciate the help.
[64:00] [Wrap-up and scheduling notes — meeting closed around 15:04 PDT (approx)]

End of transcript.
